Because your hands shake. One long exposure smears into blur.

youtube.title: Your Night Photo Isn't One Photo (Real Noise Simulation)
youtube.description:
Phone night modes capture a burst of short frames instead of one long exposure. Each short frame stays sharp but is noisy; because photon shot noise and read noise are random, averaging N aligned frames cuts the noise by the square root of N: 4 frames give half the noise, 16 frames a quarter. A long single exposure would collect the same light, but hand shake smears it into blur. Google's Night Sight (Pixel) captures up to 15 frames of up to 1/3 s each when handheld (up to 1 s each on a tripod), then aligns and merges them, rejecting pieces that don't match.
Every image here is a real numpy simulation (Poisson shot noise + 3 e- read noise); the noise numbers on screen are measured from it.
Sources: Google Research blog "Night Sight: Seeing in the Dark on Pixel Phones" (2018); Liba et al., "Handheld Mobile Photography in Very Low Light" (SIGGRAPH Asia 2019); signal averaging (SNR grows with sqrt N).
